# Phase handoff — Shared Reference — entry point handoff-to-main

This file holds entry point `handoff-to-main` of `phase-handoff`: §1, §2, §4.1, §4.2 and §4.3, and in part §4.0 ("What declining costs", "takes the strongest class" and "Classify by naming the reader"). Any other section is in the whole reference: `Skill(skill: "workflows-core:reference", args: "phase-handoff")`. This file is 348 lines long.

`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}` in this file is `workflows-core`'s root, whichever plugin's run reads it.

## 1. Hard rules

Inherited from `specs-repo-git.md` — the first three unchanged for every call against `$SPECS_PATH` (rule 1 adds only §2.7.1's two template reads, which run in the repository its caller names), and the fourth **widened** where it says so:

1. **`git -C` always; `cd` never.** Every invocation is `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" …`, save §2.7.1's two template reads, which run in the repository its caller names — `$SPECS_PATH` only for this file's own §2.7. Most callers are running inside a *different* repository; a `cd` would corrupt their git state. The `gh` calls in §2.6 and §3.5 name the repository with `-R` for the same reason.
2. **Bounded paths.** Only the calling command's own declared deliverable paths are staged, by enumeration (§2.3). `git add -A` is never issued at repository scope.
3. **Bounded branches.** Only branches matching `^(idea|prd|ard|spec|epics|design|ready|brd|frames|kb|conformance)/` are the plugin's (`specs-repo-git.md` §2.2), save the session branch, which is the plugin's for commit and push only and is never switched to here (`specs-repo-git.md` §1 rule 3).
4. **Never destructive — and this one is WIDER than the rule it inherits, deliberately.** `specs-repo-git.md` §1 rule 4 forbids `push --force`, `push -f`, `branch -D`, `merge`, `rebase`, `reset`, and deleting an `index.lock`. This rule adds **`stash`**, **`checkout --`**, **`switch --discard-changes`** and **`switch -f`**, because a deliverable commit runs where the user's own work may be uncommitted and each of those discards it silently. Same repository, two rules — so the addition is declared here rather than left for a reader to notice. Nor does this rule take the exception that one names for `specs-repo-git.md` §4 step 6's replay, which moves the checkout onto `origin`'s commits: a deliverable push rejected as non-fast-forward is reported, never replayed (§2.5). No `push --force`, no `push -f`, no `branch -D`, no `merge`, no `rebase`, no `reset`, no `stash`, no `checkout --`, no `switch --discard-changes`, no `switch -f`, and never delete an `index.lock`. §2.4's `restore --staged` is not a `reset`, for the reason `specs-repo-git.md` §1 rule 4 gives. Nothing is discarded, save by `specs-repo-git.md` §8.3's `lift`, which returns to HEAD only a session file it has just found on the session branch.

Where this reference **differs** — each difference is deliberate, and a reader who "corrects" one to match `specs-repo-git.md` breaks this contract:

5. **`require-on-main` is fatal by design.** `specs-repo-git.md` §1 rule 5 is "never fatal", which is right for bookkeeping. A gate that reports and continues is not a gate. `handoff-to-main` is *not* fatal — the deliverable is already written — but it must report the phase as **not handed off**.
6. **The `Co-Authored-By` trailer IS carried.** `specs-repo-git.md` §1 rule 6 forbids it because bookkeeping files are plugin-generated. A deliverable is authored content, and the existing handoff phases already carry the trailer.
7. **`handoff-to-main` runs only behind a user choice.** `specs-repo-git.md` §1 rule 7 is "prompt-free". Opening a pull request is outward-facing, so it is never reached except through the calling command's consent choice (§4.3).

## 2. `handoff-to-main` — the producer entry point

Called from a producing command's Handoff phase, and **only** when the user picked the branch-and-PR choice of §4.3. **A producer requests it at that consent step** — `Skill(skill: "workflows-core:reference", args: "phase-handoff handoff-to-main")` reads this entry point's own file, which holds §4.3 as well as this section — and presents §4.3's choice from that file first; this section then runs only on the choice's first option. §2.7.1 is the exception: `dev-workflows:code-handoff` §2.7 and `docs-workflows:finish-and-handoff` §5 also run it, under their own consent. **One step of it runs earlier, and it is read-only:** §2.1's push-target probe, which §4.3 runs before it presents the choice, because the probe's result decides what that section prints above the array.

### 2.1 Gate

**Run `env-check` first** (`Skill(skill: "workflows-core:reference", args: "session-hygiene env-check")`, `session-hygiene.md` §7): it sets `specs_git: misrooted` where the run no longer stands in the environment its preflight printed, which the gate below then reads.

All of: `$SPECS_PATH` is set and is an existing directory; `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" rev-parse --git-dir` succeeds; the resolved `.git` directory is **writable**; and the run carries neither `specs_git: blocked` (`specs-repo-git.md` §3.3 G0 — a commit on a detached HEAD is reachable from no ref) nor `specs_git: misrooted` (`specs-repo-git.md` §3.1 — `$SPECS_PATH` is misplaced, and a branch cut and a commit made there land in the wrong repository, or at the wrong depth of the right one; or `session-hygiene.md` §7's `env-check` or its §6's *Stop* found the run no longer in the environment it started in or recorded, and it hands off nothing more).

Gate fails on path / repo / permission grounds → report that the deliverable is written but not handed off, and stop. Gate fails on `specs_git: blocked` → re-emit that notice. Gate fails on `specs_git: misrooted` → report that the deliverable is written but not handed off, naming the flag and repeating the notice that set it — the §3.1 notice, `session-hygiene.md` §7's `Environment changed:` notice, or its §6's `RESUME_ENVIRONMENT_CHANGED:` stop line — and stop; §4.1's *Gate failed* row carries it as `Phase handoff: NOT handed off — specs_git: misrooted (<that notice's first line>)`. A run stopped at resolution never reaches a handoff, so this fires only on a run a notice let continue, or one `session-hygiene.md` §6's *Stop* sent on to its terminal phases. **Never silent** — unlike the bookkeeping steps, silence here would hide the fact that the phase did not complete.

**The push-target probe — run before the choice, and never gated on.** `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" remote get-url origin`: exit 0 with a non-empty URL sets `remote: origin`, anything else sets `remote: none`. **It runs before §4.3 presents its array, not here**: it only reads, and its result is what decides whether §4.3 prints its no-remote notice, which a probe run after the choice could never have fed. This entry point then carries the `remote` value that probe set rather than probing a second time. A specs repo with no `origin` is an ordinary state (a tree kept locally, a clone whose remote was removed), and it is deliberately **not** a gate failure: branching and committing there still does the useful half of this entry point, and a deliverable is safer on a local commit than in a working tree. What `remote: none` removes is §2.5's push and §2.6's pull request — both are skipped — so the run says so **before** the choice is presented (§4.3's notice) and reports it afterwards through §4.1's *No remote* row.

**The probe is `origin` specifically, because every later step names `origin` literally** — §2.2's `refs/remotes/origin/<name>`, §2.5's `push -u origin`, §2.6.1's `OWNER_REPO` derivation (`owner-repo`), and §3.2's `origin/<default>`. A repository whose only remote is under some other name is therefore `remote: none` for this entry point. **Probing is not optional and no earlier step stands in for it:** §2.1's four existing conditions are all satisfiable on a repository with no remote at all, so without this probe the producer offers — marked `(Recommended)` — a *"push + open PR"* option that cannot succeed, and the operator learns it only from the raw `git push` error §2.5 reports. That is the state this probe was added for, observed live.

### 2.2 Branch resolution, and the collision rule

Intended name: `<prefix>/<KEY>-<slug>`, where `<prefix>` is the caller's own (§2.9) and `<KEY>-<slug>` come from **the resolved feature folder the deliverable was written into** — never re-derived from the item title. Folder resolution already tolerates a human-adjusted slug and a stray `-`/`_` after the key, and re-deriving would produce a branch name that disagrees with the directory it commits.

**The keyless form — `kb` only.** `/harvest-decisions` and `/promote-decisions` write no feature folder, so their intended names are `kb/harvest-<YYYY-MM-DD>` and `kb/promote-<YYYY-MM-DD>`, today's date. Each stops before writing anything while any `kb/` branch is unmerged into `<default-ref>` (its Phase 0) — a second run would re-propose what the first carries, and the two pull requests would collide on the files both write — so a name that exists here is a merged one: rule 3's reuse never matches a `kb/` branch, and rule 4's lowest free suffix applies.

Collision is normal, not exceptional: `_readiness.md` is overwritten on every `/ready` run, and a `/create-prd` re-run after its pull request merged wants the same name again. `gh pr create` fails on an already-merged branch, and force-pushing and `branch -D` are both forbidden (§1 rule 4). So:

1. Test both `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" rev-parse --verify --quiet refs/heads/<name>` and `… refs/remotes/origin/<name>`. **Where only the remote-tracking ref exists, confirm it with the host** — `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" ls-remote --exit-code --heads origin refs/heads/<name>`, the probe `specs-repo-git.md` §4 step 5 uses — and treat it as absent where that exits 2: the host deleted the branch, ordinarily on merging its pull request, and no fetch here prunes the ref it leaves behind (§3.2 there fetches the default branch alone), so it would otherwise count as taken for good and send every later handoff for the key to rule 4's suffix. Any other exit, an unreachable host included, leaves the ref counted as existing, as before.
2. Neither exists → use `<name>`.
3. **At least one exists** (the local ref, the remote ref, or — the common reuse case — both) **and** it is this run's own in-progress branch — its prefix is the caller's, `specs-repo-git.md` §3.5's `branch-key` resolves it to a key in the run key set (§3.2 there — the same resolution the preflight's B3 makes, so a branch the preflight stayed on is a branch this rule reuses), and the branch is **not already merged** → **reuse it**, switching to it rather than creating it: `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" switch <name>`, or, where only `refs/remotes/origin/<name>` exists, `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" switch --no-track -c <name> origin/<name>`, for the reason *Where a new branch is cut* gives `--no-track`. **Where git refuses that switch** — ordinarily because this run changed a path the branch changed too, and git will not overwrite it — the handoff ends there on §4.1's *Switch refused* row: the run's files stay where they are, nothing is moved or removed, and git's advice — to commit or stash a tracked file, to move or remove an untracked one — is never followed on the run's account (§1 rule 4). §6.2 asks about such a branch before the run's work; the refusal remains for one it could not see — created during the run by another session — and on the producers that pass it no `prefix`.

   **Test the merge against a ref that still exists.** Resolve the branch ref first — `refs/remotes/origin/<name>` when it exists, else `refs/heads/<name>` — and ask `specs-repo-git.md` §3.5's `branch-merged <that ref>`: merged (do not reuse; fall to rule 4 and create a fresh name), or not yet merged (reuse). That entry point finds a pull request merged by squash or by rebase too, which an ancestry test alone reads as unmerged forever — the run would then switch onto a branch whose pull request had closed and call `gh pr create` on it. Its ancestry test carries `2>/dev/null` for the same reason §3.2 gives for its own probe — on a missing ref git writes `fatal: Not a valid object name`, which must not leak into the run's output.

   **Why the remote ref alone is not enough:** with GitHub's *delete branch on merge* — the ordinary configuration — a merged branch's **remote** ref is gone while the **local** one survives. Probing only `refs/remotes/origin/<name>` then exits 128, which reads as "not yet merged", so the run switches onto a merged branch and calls `gh pr create` — the failure this section's own premise names ("`gh pr create` fails on an already-merged branch"). `specs-repo-git.md`'s B2 asks the same question, through the same entry point, against a ref that exists, and the two must not disagree about which ref to test.
4. Otherwise → append the lowest free integer suffix, starting at `-2`, retesting both refs each time as rule 1 tests them. Report the substitution in the §4.1 outcome line, because a branch name the user did not expect is a branch name they will not find.

**Where a new branch is cut.** First note the branch HEAD stands on, `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" symbolic-ref --short HEAD`, which §2.3 returns to where this run then has nothing to commit. A name rule 2 or rule 4 creates is cut at HEAD where HEAD is the default branch, or a named branch the plugin does not manage (`specs-repo-git.md` §3.3 G2), as it always was. Where HEAD is another plugin branch — the preflight's B3 keeps a run on any unmerged plugin branch its key names (`specs-repo-git.md` §3.5), whatever phase opened it — it is cut at `<default-ref>` (§3.2) instead, `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" switch --no-track -c <name> <default-ref>`, **unless that branch changed a file this run builds on**: a path it declares (§2.9), or a file it read as an input (§2.9's `inputs_read`) — every file under `$SPECS_PATH` outside `specs-repo-git.md` §2.1's session-file shapes that this run or an agent it dispatched read, whatever its kind: a PRD, an ARD, a specification, a design, an Epic, a seed, a register, a ledger, a grounding file, a frame set's files — tested with `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" diff --quiet <default-ref>...HEAD -- <those paths>`. **The three dots are load-bearing**: they compare HEAD with the point it forked from, so the test sees what that branch changed and never what the default branch changed since, which would stack a run on a branch that touched none of its files. **`--no-track` is too**: wherever there is a remote, `<default-ref>` is a remote-tracking branch, and a switch that tracked it would write the default branch into `.git/config` as the new branch's upstream — a push to the wrong branch where that file is writable, and, where a container mounts it read-only, the ordinary case §2.5 names, a switch git refuses after creating the branch. **Where the test exits non-zero the run builds on that branch's work** — `/create-ard` stamping the grounding findings an unmerged `/prd-ground` branch wrote, `/epics` partitioning a PRD whose pull request is still open, `/dev-workflows:design` reading the target an unmerged `/epics` refinement set — so its branch is cut at HEAD, a stack that states the dependency honestly (`specs-repo-git.md` §3.6), and §4.1's *Stacked on another phase's branch* clause says so on the outcome line — merging that pull request lands the other phase's commits too, and the operator meets that before merging it rather than after. **Cutting at HEAD everywhere made a pull request carry another phase's unmerged commits it does not depend on**: a PRD-level `/update-prd` run while `/epics`' pull request was open cut `prd/` from `epics/`, so merging the PRD would have landed the Epic drafts unreviewed with it. The switch carries this run's uncommitted deliverable with it. **Where git refuses it** — a file it would overwrite, such as a session file both this run and that branch's terminal commit appended to — cut at HEAD instead, as before this rule, and append §4.1's *Stacked on another phase's branch* clause to its outcome line, so the operator who opens the pull request sees the stack before merging it.

**In session-branch mode** (`specs-repo-git.md` §8), the switch onto `<name>` — creating it or reusing it — is wrapped in that section's `lift` and `put-back` (§8.3); a `lift` that skips the move refuses the handoff with the reason, as a failed switch does.

### 2.3 Staging the deliverable

Staging is by enumeration, never by glob — the same discipline as `specs-repo-git.md` §2.1, applied to a different path set:

1. `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" status --porcelain -z --untracked-files=all`. `--untracked-files=all` is **required**: the default collapses an untracked directory to a single `?? dir/` line, hiding which files are staged.
2. Classify each reported path against the caller's declared deliverable paths (§2.9). Everything else is **OTHER** and is never staged — including the `dev-workflows/**` bookkeeping paths, which belong to `commit-artifacts`.
3. `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" add -A -- <path> [<path>…]` with the literal paths. `-A` is used deliberately: a producer may delete a file it relocated (`/update-prd` supersedes a revision), and that deletion must be staged. `-A` states the intent explicitly and was strictly required before git 2.0; on git ≥ 2.0 a plain `git add -- <path>` stages a deletion for a literal path too — verified empirically — so keep `-A`, but do not justify it by claiming plain `git add` cannot stage the deletion.
4. **Account for every declared path.** Each path §2.9 declared is now either staged by step 3, or reported by no record at all. A path with no record is **accounted for only where it is already on the branch unchanged**: `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" cat-file -t "HEAD:<path>" 2>/dev/null` prints `blob`. No record means the worktree, the index and `HEAD` agree, so a path `HEAD` carries as a blob is committed and byte-identical to what this phase wrote. Anything else — a non-zero exit, or an output of `tree` — is named in §4.1's *declaration unaccounted for* clause: a path nothing wrote, one git ignores, and the shapes nothing could place — a declaration given as an absolute path, as a directory, or as a glob. A **record** step 2 could not read as a path is not a declared path at all and has none to substitute, so it takes §4.1's *record unreadable* clause instead, which quotes the record. **Do not test existence under `$SPECS_PATH` in its place.** A re-run re-copies a file byte-for-byte — every file under `/brd-intake`'s `brd/source/`, `/idea`'s vendored sources, a `/frames` index rebuilt verbatim — so it exists, stages nothing, and is already on the branch; an existence test names each one as NOT on a branch it is on, which is the commonest benign path there is, and the clause then reads as noise on the runs it was built to be read on. Measured on git 2.43.0 against a two-run `/brd-intake` folder: the existence test fired on every committed, unchanged path — the noise above — and missed a declaration given as a **directory**, which `-e` finds; this test stays silent on those paths and reports the directory as `tree`. Nothing this step cannot place is dropped in silence — which is the half of the defect *What this closes* records that `-z` alone does not buy: the drop had no voice, so the run reported a handoff it had not made. This does not stop the entry point: the paths that did stage are still committed, pushed and opened as a pull request, and the clause is what tells the operator which declared artifact is not among them.

**`-z` is required, and `specs-repo-git.md` §2.1 is where the hazard it answers is stated.** That section names it twice for its own classifier — `git status --porcelain` wraps a path carrying a space, a `"`, a `\` or a non-ASCII byte in double quotes and octal-escapes the non-ASCII bytes, and a classifier anchored at `^` and reading the path as reported never matches it. §2.1's step 1 reads `-z` for that reason and so does this one, over a different path set. The difference worth keeping in view is that §2.1 can also **constrain the paths it owns** — it flattens `<docs-repo-slug>` to a single segment of safe bytes — while a deliverable path here need not be the plugin's to shape at all: `/brd-intake` copies a customer's linked files under the names the customer gave them, and `/idea` vendors a designer's exports under theirs. Under `-z` each record is terminated by a NUL and the path is emitted raw: strip the two status bytes and the space from the front of a record and the remainder is the path, byte for byte as declared. A **rename or copy** record carries a second NUL-terminated field, the original path, straight after it (`R  <new>\0<old>\0`) — consume it with the record it belongs to, never as a record of its own, which has no status bytes to strip. `-c core.quotepath=false` is **not** the fix and must not be substituted for `-z`: it suppresses only the octal escaping, and a path carrying a space is still quoted.

**What this closes.** Until `-z` was read here, a declared deliverable whose filename carried a space or a non-ASCII byte was reported quoted, matched no declared path, fell to **OTHER**, and was never staged — while the run reported the handoff as done. That is the silent-and-total failure the paragraph below names for an *undeclared* path, reached by a second route: the path was declared, and the classifier could not see that it was.

**A declared path is always a file, never a directory and never a glob.** Step 2 classifies each
reported path against the declaration, so a directory in the list would leave every file under it
ambiguous — matched by a reader who expands it, OTHER by one who does not. A caller whose phase writes
a set of files rather than one (`/idea` vendors its sources into `attachments/` and
`design/<frame-set>/` — `product-workflows:idea-format`, *Vendored sources*;
`/frames` writes one `index.md` per `design/*/` set of the folder it resolved —
`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/grounding-format.md` §6.2) enumerates every one of them literally. The consequence of leaving one out is silent and total: it is
classified OTHER, never staged, and never reaches the default branch, while the deliverable that links
it lands there pointing at a path on no ref.

**Nothing staged → no commit**, and what follows turns on the branch §2.2 settled:

- **A branch §2.2 created in this run** (rule 2 or rule 4) holds no commit of its own, so it is removed rather than left empty: switch back to the branch §2.2 noted before cutting it — in session-branch mode wrapped in `specs-repo-git.md` §8.3's `lift` and `put-back`, as §2.2's switch is — and run `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" branch -d <branch>`, never `-D` (§1 rule 4), so the run's session files land where they would have without a handoff. Where git refuses the switch, or the `-d` — a branch cut at `<default-ref>` that the branch the run returns to does not hold reads as not fully merged — keep the branch, stay where git left the run, and the line names it: one the `-d` left holds no commit of its own, and a later run's preflight standing on `<default>` deletes it (`specs-repo-git.md` §3.4); on one the switch back left, the run's session files land on the cut branch (`specs-repo-git.md` §4.1). §2.5 and §2.6 are skipped.
- **A reused branch** (§2.2 rule 3) is re-published where `remote: origin` holds and the branch carries a commit that `<default-ref>` lacks, that `origin`'s copy of the branch lacks too, and that is not a session-file commit as `specs-repo-git.md` §4 step 5's `push-scope` tests one — a deliverable an earlier handoff committed and could not push, or a merge of the default branch the operator made on row B′'s remedy. `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" rev-list refs/heads/<branch> --not <default-ref> refs/remotes/origin/<branch>` lists the candidates, the last ref named only where §2.2 rule 1 counted it. §2.5 and §2.6 then run as after a commit, and their §4.1 row is the line. Otherwise both are skipped, and a branch already on `origin` keeps the pull request it has.

Where §2.5 does not run, emit §4.1's *Nothing to commit* line. It says where the deliverable is, which is what the next phase's gate tests (§3), by two tests over the declared paths on the branch the run now stands on: **already on `<default>`** where `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" diff --quiet <default-ref> -- <the declared paths>` exits 0; **on that branch, unmerged**, where `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" diff --quiet <default-ref>...HEAD -- <the declared paths>` exits 1, the branch having changed them; and otherwise **changed on `<default>` after that branch was cut**, which the branch has not taken in — row B′'s first finding (§3.3) — save where that branch is the default branch itself (`git -C "$SPECS_PATH" symbolic-ref --short HEAD` prints `<default>`), whose local copy is then **behind `<default-ref>`**, as where the catch-up (`specs-repo-git.md` §3.4) could not run. This is not an error: a re-run that changed nothing is a legitimate outcome.

### 2.4 Commit

Message `<KEY> <summary>`, matching the specs repo's own `<KEY|NOISSUE> <summary>` convention. Carry `Co-Authored-By: <the session model's name> <noreply@anthropic.com>` (§1 rule 6).

**Commit by pathspec, never the index** — the paths §2.3 step 3 staged that git still lists as staged, and nothing else, listed, committed and followed by the index restore exactly as `specs-repo-git.md` §4 step 4 does, with this phase's message. A plain `git commit` takes whatever the index holds, and a change the user had staged in the specs repository rides §2.2's switch onto this branch and would land in the deliverable's commit; where the list is empty, there is nothing to commit, and §2.3's *Nothing staged* paragraph applies. Once the list holds a path, write the message to a `command mktemp -t dw-handoff-msg-XXXXXX` file outside any repository — that `mktemp` run with `TMPDIR` set to the session's scratchpad directory where the session names one that exists — and commit with `-F <msg-path>` rather than `-m`, because `<summary>` is free text and a double-quoted `-m` command-substitutes its backticks and `$(…)` before git sees it; remove the file once the commit has been made or has failed, with `command rm -f -- "<msg-path>"`. A commit git refuses — a hook's rejection, a signature it cannot make, a merge in progress — is reported through §4.1's *Commit failed* row, never retried and never run with `--no-verify`.

### 2.5 Push

**This step runs only where §2.4 made the commit, or §2.3 found a reused branch's commit to re-publish.** The push is a shell command of its own, run once the commit's exit status has been read — never chained after the commit in one command line, and never after a construct that swallows the commit's failure (`rc=$?`, `|| true`, `;`). A live `/specify` handoff ran the switch, the add, the commit and the push as one command that kept the commit's status in `rc=$?`, so when a `pre-commit` hook refused the commit, it still pushed an empty `spec/` branch at the default branch's tip. Where neither holds — nothing to commit and nothing to re-publish (§2.3), or a commit git refused (§4.1's *Commit failed*) — nothing is pushed, and §2.6 is skipped with it: a pull request needs a pushed head.

`git -C "$SPECS_PATH" push -u origin <branch>`. Never force. A non-fast-forward rejection is reported, never resolved by rebasing or forcing mid-run.

**A push refused for access leaves a commit the operator pushes.** Where git's error says this identity may not write to `origin` — `Permission denied`, `Permission to <repo> denied`, `denied to <user>`, or an HTTP `403` — the identity can fetch and not push, which no retry within the run changes. §4.1's *Push refused for access* row names the branch and the commit left on it and gives the exact push to run once access is fixed; the run asks nothing and tries no other credentials.

**A `.git/config` git cannot write costs `-u` its upstream, never the push.** A container that mounts the file read-only is the ordinary case. git pushes, exits 0, and then prints `error: could not write config file <path>: …` or `error: could not lock config file <path>: …` — on a read-only mount it may still announce that the branch is "set up to track" — and records no upstream. That is not a failed push and needs no investigation: the outcome is the push's exit status and its `-> <branch>` line, which §4.1's pushed rows report, and the run says nothing more about it. This reference reads no upstream; `specs-repo-git.md` §4 step 5 tests for one, and falls back to the remote-tracking ref the push wrote where there is none.

**Skipped entirely where §2.1 set `remote: none`**, and §2.6 is skipped with it — a pull request needs a pushed head. The commit §2.4 made still stands; §4.1's *No remote* row reports it, and the phase is described as **not handed off** exactly as §2.8 requires of every other way the push can fail to land.

### 2.6 Open the pull request

Not reached where §2.1 set `remote: none` — §2.5 pushed nothing, and `gh` has no head branch to open a pull request from — nor where §2.5 did not run for want of a commit to push (§2.5): this run pushed nothing, and a reused branch already on `origin` keeps the pull request it has (§2.3).

**First, derive `$OWNER_REPO`**, by §2.6.1's `owner-repo`; where it finds the remote no `gh` target, skip to §4.2 without calling `gh`.

**Then probe for an existing pull request** — this entry point's §2.2 rule 3 deliberately *reuses* an in-progress branch, and §2.2 says in as many words that collision is normal rather than exceptional, so a branch that already carries a pull request is the ordinary case here:

    gh pr list -R "$OWNER_REPO" --head <branch> --state open --json number,url

One already open ⇒ §2.5's push has already updated it. Report it through §4.1's *already existed* row and do **not** call `gh pr create`, which fails on the duplicate and would send the run down §4.2 telling the user to open a pull request that exists. This is the same primitive §3.5 already uses on the consumer side.

Otherwise: run a cheap `gh auth status` pre-check purely to avoid a confusing raw error, then call `gh` with every argument that would otherwise make it prompt — the plugin must never block on an interactive editor:

    gh pr create -R "$OWNER_REPO" --base <default> --head <branch> \
                 --title '<title>' --body-file <body-path>

**`<title>` is free text, so it goes in single quotes**, each `'` it holds written `'\''`: inside double quotes its backticks and `$(…)` would be command-substituted before `gh` saw it.

**Capability probe, not host classification.** Try the call; on any failure fall back to §4.2's instruction. Push authority and pull-request authority are independent — push runs over SSH with a per-repo key, `gh` runs over the API with a token, and the same account can have write access to one repository and read access to another. No hostname or host-type test can detect that mismatch, so a run can push successfully and still be unable to open the pull request. This is why `docs-workflows:finish-and-handoff` §4's host classification is right for choosing *instructions* and insufficient here.

`gh` wraps the API rather than calling it over HTTPS, which is what the zero-direct-API rule permits — the same allowance `/document` already relies on.

### 2.6.1 `owner-repo` — deriving $OWNER_REPO

`$OWNER_REPO` is the `[HOST/]OWNER/REPO` value a `gh -R` call names, derived from a repository's `origin` remote — §2.6's calls and §3.5's probe name the specs repo's. This block derives it from `$SPECS_PATH`'s `origin`; a reader that derives it for another repository reads that repository's `origin` in its place:

    url=$(git -C "$SPECS_PATH" remote get-url origin)
    host=$(printf '%s' "$url" | sed -E 's#^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9+.-]*://##; s#^[^/@]+@##; s#[:/].*$##')
    slug=$(printf '%s' "$url" | sed -E 's#^[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z0-9+.-]*://##; s#^[^/@]+@##; s#^[^/:]+(:[0-9]+)?[/:]##; s#/+$##; s#\.git$##')
    case "$url" in
      http://*|https://*) ;;
      *) case "$host" in
           github.com) ;;
           [A-Za-z0-9]*) real=$(ssh -G "$host" 2>/dev/null | awk '$1=="hostname" {print $2; exit}')
                         case "$real" in ssh.github.com) host=github.com ;; ?*) host=$real ;; esac ;;
         esac ;;
    esac
    case "$host" in github.com) OWNER_REPO="$slug" ;; *) OWNER_REPO="$host/$slug" ;; esac

**An SSH host alias is resolved before the host is kept.** An scp-like or `ssh://` remote may name a `Host` alias from `~/.ssh/config` — `git@github-ig.com:owner/repo.git`, whose `HostName` is `github.com` — which only ssh knows: `gh` reads `-R` as a real host, so `github-ig.com/owner/repo` failed every `gh` call with `error connecting to github-ig.com` while the push over the same alias succeeded (measured). `ssh -G <host>` prints the configuration ssh would use and connects to nothing; its `hostname` line is the real host, and the host itself where no alias applies. An `http(s)://` remote names a real host and is left alone, and so is `github.com` itself, which GitHub's documented port-443 setup (`Host github.com` / `Hostname ssh.github.com`) would otherwise rename; a resolved `ssh.github.com` reads as `github.com`. Only a plain hostname is passed to `ssh`, so the remote's text can never reach it as an option; and where `ssh` is absent or prints no `hostname`, the host stands as written.

**The host is kept, not stripped** — the same rule as `dev-workflows:code-handoff` §2.6, and for the same reason. `gh -R` accepts `[HOST/]OWNER/REPO`, and `gh auth status` succeeds whenever the user is authenticated to *any* host, so a bare `OWNER/REPO` derived from a GitHub Enterprise remote resolves against **github.com** — silently opening the phase's pull request on an unrelated public repository if one happens to sit at that path, with §2.6's capability probe catching nothing because the call succeeded. Only `github.com` may drop the host. Validate the slug against `^[^/]+/[^/]+$` before calling `gh`; anything else (a Bitbucket `scm/proj/repo`, a nested GitLab group) is not a `gh` target, and no `gh` call is made against it — `handoff-to-main` skips to §4.2 (§2.6), and §3.5 skips its probe. §3.5's `gh pr list -R "$OWNER_REPO"` uses the same value and mistargets identically without this.

The expressions strip a scheme, a `user@`, and a host with an optional `:port` terminated by `/` or `:` (the scp-like `git@host:Org/repo` form uses a colon), then a trailing slash and `.git`. The earlier two-expression form handled only `git@host:` and `https://host/`, and passed an `ssh://git@host/Org/repo.git` remote through unchanged — `gh` then failed on a repository argument that was a whole URL. Do not simplify it back.

### 2.7 Title and body

Title: the `title` input (§2.9), which §2.4's commit subject also is — on a re-publish (§2.3), which makes no commit, the input alone.

Body: written to a file (never passed inline, which would break on newlines and quoting) containing what the phase produced; the artifact paths; the reviewer verdict where the caller has one; the count of open questions or `[NEEDS CLARIFICATION]` markers; and, **where the caller has one**, the next command in the chain together with the fact that it will not run on what this pull request carries until the pull request is merged — it stops on a new artifact sitting on this branch (§3.3 rows D and E), the owner of the branch included, while on an artifact the default branch already carries it meets the default branch's copy, without this run's edit, and stops on the difference or reads that copy (§3.3's A and C rows), save a consumer sharing the producer's prefix and key, which row B lets read the branch's copy, so a producer whose set may hold either says which, per artifact, by the same `<default-ref>` test that picks its consent array (§4.1), as `/epics` does — scoped exactly as the reviewer verdict beside it is, because a producer whose artifact has no §3.4 row has no next command to name and cannot render this sentence without inventing one. Where `$SPECS_PATH`'s repository carries a pull-request template, the body is that template filled with these facts (§2.7.1).

### 2.7.1 The repository's own pull-request template

**Where the repository a pull request is opened in carries a template, the body is that template, filled.** This subsection is the one statement of that rule. This reference's §2.7 applies it in `$SPECS_PATH`, `dev-workflows:code-handoff` §2.7 in a code repository, and `docs-workflows:finish-and-handoff` §5 in a docs repository. Each caller supplies `<repo>`, its own body's sections in their order, and any line that must come first (a banner).

**Resolve the template against a fixed set of paths, never by searching for one.** List the committed tree's candidates with `git -C "<repo>" ls-tree -r -z --full-tree --name-only HEAD | tr '\0' '\n' | grep -i -E '^(\.github/|docs/)?pull_request_template(\.md|/[^/]+\.md)$|^\.gitlab/merge_request_templates/default\.md$'`. Use `-z` because, without it, git quotes a name holding a non-ASCII byte and the anchor never matches it, and `--full-tree` so the listing is the whole tree wherever `<repo>` points. No output is no template. Otherwise stop at the first rung below that a listed path matches, comparing without regard to case:

1. `.github/pull_request_template.md`, then `pull_request_template.md` at the root, then `docs/pull_request_template.md`;
2. the first of `.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/`, `PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/` and `docs/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/` that holds a `.md` file directly: where it holds exactly one, that file; where it holds several, none — a directory of templates names no default, so the body takes the caller's own shape and its last line says the repository offers several templates, naming the directory;
3. `.gitlab/merge_request_templates/Default.md`.

**Read the template with `git -C "<repo>" show HEAD:<path>`**, `<path>` spelled exactly as the listing printed it (git looks a path up case-sensitively). Read the committed file, never a working-tree copy, which may hold somebody else's edit.

**Fill it:**
- keep its headings in their order, and answer each section from the facts the caller's own body carries;
- a section the run has nothing for says so and why, and never keeps the template's placeholder text;
- tick a checkbox only where the run can show what it claims, and never delete one;
- place each section of the caller's own body in the template section that asks for it, and append every one no template section asks for after the template, in the caller's order;
- a template with no headings is one section, answered in place;
- an HTML comment (`<!-- … -->`) in a template is its note to whoever fills it: follow it, then remove it with the placeholder text;
- the caller's required first line stays the first line.

**The template wins because the body replaces it otherwise.** `gh pr create --body-file` replaces what the web UI would have prefilled, and a body the user pastes by hand replaces it too, so a body in the caller's own shape would delete the template on either path.

### 2.8 Failure discipline

Every failure is reported and the phase is described as **not handed off**. The run is not retroactively failed — the deliverable is written and intact — but no report may imply the handoff succeeded. The next phase's gate is what enforces the consequence.

### 2.9 Caller-supplied inputs

| Input | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `prefix` | one of `idea`, `prd`, `ard`, `spec`, `epics`, `design`, `ready`, `brd` (shared by every `/brd-*` command and, on the BRD route, `/prd-ground`, the way `prd` is shared by `/create-prd`, `/update-prd`, `/prd-proposal`, `/docs-workflows:release-notes` and, on the idea route, `/prd-ground`), `frames`, `kb`, `conformance` (`/dev-workflows:conformance`, for its `_conformance.md` record and the `## Engineering review` notes it writes) |
| `feature_folder` | the resolved directory the deliverable was written into — none for `kb` (§2.2's keyless form) |
| `deliverable_paths` | the literal repo-relative paths this phase wrote — authored or copied in — one file each, never a directory (§2.3); the proposal commands also declare the shared proposal profile on every run, written or not, which §2.3 step 4 accounts for where the branch already carries it unchanged (§4.0) |
| `title` | the commit subject and pull-request title |
| `body_facts` | what §2.7 renders |
| `inputs_read` | every file under `$SPECS_PATH` outside `specs-repo-git.md` §2.1's session-file shapes that this run or an agent it dispatched read — §2.2's stack test reads it beside `deliverable_paths`. Derived by the run from its own reads rather than declared ahead, and recorded as it reads, so a compacted context still holds it |

### 4.0 The three downstream classes

`<downstream-clause>` (§4.1), `<next-phase-clause>` (§4.1) and the consent array (§4.3) all answer one question about the artifact the producer has just written — **what does not landing it cost?** — and all three must answer it the same way. There are **three** answers, not two — and the **gated** one splits again at reporting time, on §3.4's own column, into the two `<next-phase-clause>` values §4.1 fixes and the two §4.3 arrays that pair with them. **Three is the class count and never the array count**: reading it as both is how §4.3 came to carry three arrays against §4.1's four.

| Class | The test | What declining costs |
|---|---|---|
| **gated** | a consumer runs `require-on-main` on it — §3.4's table has a row naming it — or a consumer's own guard stops while it is uncommitted | that consumer's own §3.4 behaviour: a stop for most rows, a delegated fallback for the rows that preserve one; for a guard, a stop; and, where the run edited a copy the default branch already carries, the C rows' stop whatever the rows say (§4.1) |
| **advisory** | no §3.4 row, **but** a command reads the artifact and never gates on it | nothing stops **because of the decline**. The reader reads the working copy, so it still sees this run's result — the artifact is unshared, not blocking. **"Nothing stops" is about the handoff, not about the file's contents**: a consumer may perfectly well refuse what it finds inside an advisory artifact (`/prd-ground` stops on a moved pin recorded in `grounding/baselines.md`; `/epics` on a `prd.md` stating no requirements), and that is a different question from whether the artifact reached the default branch |
| **unread** | no §3.4 row and no reader after the run that wrote it — none downstream, and no later run of the producing command | nothing |

**What this table is, and what it is not.** It classifies every artifact the tree's `deliverable_paths` declarations name — derived from those declarations rather than from memory, which is the direction that had never been walked: the table carried twelve rows against roughly thirty declared paths, and most of the missing ones rode in a set that already held a gated path and were carried by the strongest-class rule, which is why their absence had cost nothing until `/prd-ground --no-code` produced the first set with no classified path in it at all. **Treat an unlisted path as unclassified rather than as unread**, name its reader, add its row, and only then pick the array. A producer adding a deliverable adds its row here in the same change.

**A handoff whose `deliverable_paths` set spans classes takes the strongest class in it** — **gated** if any one path is gated, otherwise **advisory** if any one is advisory. One array is presented for one handoff, and it has to state the largest thing declining costs: an operator told "no command stops on this" about a set containing a gated artifact will meet the stop anyway. `/brd-reconcile`'s two handoffs are the live case, and they differ: its first hands off the returned review alone (advisory), its second hands that review off together with `decisions.md` and `coverage-ledger.md`, both gated — so the second is gated even though one path in it is not.

**Classify by naming the reader, never by the absence of a §3.4 row.** A missing row rules out `require-on-main` gating and settles nothing else: it says no consumer gates the artifact through §3.4 — a consumer's own guard can still stop on it, as on `architecture/**` — and says nothing at all about whether it is *read*. Conflating the two is what shipped — §4.3's second array told the operator that nothing downstream reads the artifact it was selected for, while `/implement` Phase 0.5 was reading `_readiness.md` on every keyed run. So: a §3.4 row, or a consumer's own guard that stops on it ⇒ **gated**; neither ⇒ name the command and the phase that reads it, and where one can be named the class is **advisory**, where none can it is **unread**. Adding a reader for an artifact adds its row to the table above; a reader that becomes a gate moves the artifact into §3.4 and out of it.

### 4.1 `handoff-to-main` outcome line

Exactly one, prefixed `Phase handoff:`, **per handoff the run offers** — one line per run for
every producer but one.

**Every row here is an outcome of a handoff that was *offered*, and a run prints one line for each
handoff it offered, whichever way each went.** A decline is inside that scope and not outside it —
options 2 and 3 both decline, `handoff-to-main` never executes, and the *Declined by the user* row
below is still the line, emitted by the **producer** (§4.3's *What each option means* is the
authority on that). The heading names the entry point because the other rows are its outcomes; the
count is per **offer**, not per execution of §2.

**A run that never reaches an offer prints no line for it, and the absence of a row for that state
is deliberate.** A producer may skip its handoff on a condition of its own — `/frames` writes no
index and so has no deliverable to hand off, `/idea` on `status: draft` never hands off and does not
ask, `/implement`'s Phase 4.5 is a silent no-op where step 7.5 wrote no conformance note in `$SPECS_PATH`, or where the run is a direct one from inside the specs repository and its notes ride on the code commit, and
`/brd-proposal` writes nothing where its readiness walk ends on *Price the slice first* or *Re-price
it first* — and there the *Declined by the user* row would assert a decision nobody was asked to
make.

**One producer offers two handoffs, and it prints two lines.** `/brd-reconcile` hands off the
returned customer review it canonicalised, then its own reconciliation record on the branch that
first handoff created (§2.2 rule 3): two deliverables, two consent choices, two outcomes that can
differ — so one line cannot report both, and collapsing them would drop whichever it did not report.
**Where a run offers more than one handoff, each line names which handoff it reports**, as that
command already does. It is the only such producer today; every other command in the family offers
`handoff-to-main` **at most** once — at most, because a producer may reach no offer at all (the
skips named above are examples of that, not its whole extent: a run that stops before its handoff
phase reaches none either), and because a declined offer still prints its line while §2 never runs —
so for them the per-offer count and the per-run count are the same number, which is why this rule
read "one per run" until a run emitted two.

**A consent choice asked again supersedes its earlier answer's line.** Where the run asks one offer's §4.3 choice a second time — an interrupted answer put again — the line for the earlier answer is void: the run prints the line for the last answer, and its report carries that line alone for the offer, never both, so a run never reports one offer as both declined and handed off.

**Three states, and a producer settles which each of its handoffs is in before printing**: offered
and taken, offered and declined, never offered — a line for the first two, none for the third, once
per offer. All three have been misread in shipped text, in three different directions: a prose
alternative in place of the line on a decline, a demand for the line on a run that never offered
one, and two lines on a run whose reader expected one.

| Case | Line |
|---|---|
| Committed, pushed, PR opened | `Phase handoff: <branch> pushed — PR #<n> open (<url>). <downstream-clause>` |
| PR already existed | `Phase handoff: <branch> pushed to existing PR #<n> (<url>). <downstream-clause>` |
| PR not opened | `Phase handoff: <branch> pushed — PR NOT opened (<reason>). Open it manually. <downstream-clause>` |
| Push failed | `Phase handoff: committed <sha7> on <branch> — push FAILED (<reason>). The phase is NOT handed off; <sha7> stays on local <branch>. Once the cause is fixed, run git -C "<SPECS_PATH>" push -u origin <branch>, then open its pull request into <default>; a later handoff of <branch> re-publishes it too (§2.3).` |
| Push refused for access (§2.5) | `Phase handoff: committed <sha7> on <branch> — push REFUSED: this identity may not push to origin (<git's first error line>). The phase is NOT handed off; <sha7> stays on local <branch>. Once you have push access, run git -C "<SPECS_PATH>" push -u origin <branch>, then open its pull request into <default>.` |
| No remote | `Phase handoff: committed <sha7> on <branch> — this specs repo has no origin remote, so nothing was pushed and no PR was opened. The phase is NOT handed off.` |
| Nothing to commit | `Phase handoff: no deliverable changes to commit on <branch><, which this run cut and has removed \| , which this run cut and left in place, holding no commit of its own, since git would not delete it (<git's first line>) — a later run standing on <default> deletes it \| , which this run cut and stays on, since git refused the switch back (<git's first line>) \| >. Nothing was pushed, and no pull request was opened; the deliverable <is already on <default> \| sits on <current>, unmerged \| changed on <default> after <current> was cut, and <current> has not changed it \| changed on <default-ref>, which your local <default> is behind>.` — `<current>` the branch the run stands on (§2.3) |
| Commit failed | `Phase handoff: NOT handed off — the commit failed (<the first line of git's error or the hook's output>). The deliverable is staged on <branch>, not committed. Nothing was pushed, and no pull request was opened.` |
| Branch name substituted | append `; branch name <intended> was taken, used <actual>` — never to a *Nothing to commit* line whose branch §2.3 removed |
| Stacked on another phase's branch | append `; cut from <HEAD's branch>, whose unmerged commits this pull request carries — <it changed <path>, which this run builds on \| git refused the switch to <default-ref>: <git's first line>>` (§2.2, *Where a new branch is cut*) — never to a *Nothing to commit* line, which opens no pull request — naming, where it stacked on purpose, the first path `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" diff --name-only <default-ref>...HEAD -- <the tested paths>` prints |
| Declaration unaccounted for | append `; <path> was declared but staged by nothing — this run put nothing on <branch> for it` (§2.3 step 4), one clause per path |
| Record unreadable | append `; a status record could not be read as a path (<record>) — nothing was staged for it` (§2.3 step 4), one clause per record |
| Declined by the user | `Phase handoff: skipped at your request — this run's deliverable (<artifacts>) is written but not on <default>. <next-phase-clause>` |
| Gate failed | `Phase handoff: NOT handed off — <reason>` |
| Switch refused (§2.2 rule 3) | `Phase handoff: refused — git would not switch to <branch> (<git's first line>)<, naming <paths>, which this run changed and <branch> changed too | >. Nothing was committed, pushed or opened, and nothing was moved or removed: the deliverable stays written and uncommitted on <current>. Merge <branch>'s pull request, or close it and delete <branch> from this clone and from origin, then re-run this command.` — `<paths>` the paths git listed where its refusal names files it would overwrite, up to eight and `…and <n> more` |

**The *Declined by the user* row names the whole declared set.** `<artifacts>` is every path of the run's `deliverable_paths` (§2.9), comma-separated, where it declared three or fewer; beyond three it is `<n> files under <dir>`, `<n>` the number declared and `<dir>` the nearest directory holding every declared path, repo-relative — the `feature_folder` where every path sits inside it, and a directory above it where the set spans folders, as `/brd-reconcile`'s second handoff does when it declares the parent's defect log or a dependent BRD's `decisions.md`, and `/brd-interview`'s when it declares the parent's defect log. A decline stages nothing, so the declaration is the only list there is, and a line naming one file of a twenty-five-file set tells the operator who has just taken git into their own hands about one of the twenty-five. The line's subject is singular whatever the count — *this run's deliverable* — so every `<next-phase-clause>` value can call it *it*, and the clause always opens a sentence there: each value listed below is written capitalised for that reason.

**A re-publish (§2.3) prints the row its push and pull request reach**, `<sha7>` there being the branch's tip, since this run committed nothing, and names no path beneath it.

**Every committed path is named, beneath the line.** On each row that committed something — *Committed, pushed, PR opened*, *PR already existed*, *PR not opened*, *Push failed*, *Push refused for access*, *No remote* — follow the outcome line with one indented line per path §2.4's commit carried (the paths §2.3 step 3 staged that git still listed as staged), in the order step 3 staged them, each written exactly as git reported it under `-z` (raw, never re-quoted). Above eight, print the first eight and `…and <n> more`; on the rows that open a pull request, §2.7's body file carries the **declared** set, which is not the staged set in exactly the case step 4 exists for. The line itself stays one line, so the rule above is intact. This is the positive half of §2.3 step 4 and it is what made the quoted-path defect survive releases: nothing printed which paths landed, so nothing revealed that one had not. An operator who reads the list against the artifact they just wrote sees a missing name in the place they are already looking.

**`<downstream-clause>` is resolved from §4.0's class, on the same principle as the array.** On a **gated** artifact it is `The next phase runs once it is merged.` — or, on the *PR not opened* row, `The next phase will stop until it is merged.` On an **advisory** one it is `No command waits on this; what reads it reads it as advice.` On an **unread** one it is `Nothing downstream reads it, so no command waits on this.` These are the *success* path, and before this clause existed they asserted a waiting phase unconditionally — so a `/frames` run that handed off cleanly printed "The next phase runs once it is merged." having, in the same phase, just offered the §4.3 array that says nothing reads it. Both halves of that run were wrong, and it took two fixes to see it: the clause was corrected first, and the array it was made to agree with was itself wrong — a frame-set index is read (§4.0), so `/frames` is **advisory**. A run must not contradict its own prompt, and the outcome line is the half the operator acts on. The *No remote*, *Push failed* and *Push refused for access* rows carry no clause at all: none landed the artifact, so the sentence to print about what happens next is the same one the *Declined by the user* row prints, and repeating it beside "The phase is NOT handed off." would say twice what that row already says once.

**`<next-phase-clause>` resolves four ways: §4.0's three classes, with the *gated* one split by §3.4's own column.** Declining writes no branch and no commit, so a gated artifact's next phase reads **row F** — where the artifact was on no ref before this run, as *Row F is the next phase's reading only where …* below says — or, for a guard, finds the uncommitted copy it stops on — row F delegates, and §3.4 records per consumer whether that delegation is a stop or a fallback. **The split is a quantifier over that artifact's rows, never a choice of consumer**: most gated artifacts have several §3.4 rows and some have both kinds, so "the row for that consumer" leaves a run with two defensible clauses and no tie-break. The four, and §4.3 carries one array per value:

- **gated — stopping** (§4.3's first array), where **any** §3.4 row naming the artifact says *stops*, or a consumer's own guard stops on it → `The next phase will stop until it is.` One stopping row is enough, on the same strongest-consequence principle §4.0's set rule follows: an operator told nothing stops who then meets one has lost a run, where an over-warned operator has lost nothing.
- **gated — falling back** (§4.3's second array), where **every** §3.4 row naming it preserves a pre-existing absent behaviour → `The next phase does not stop on that: it falls back to what it does when the deliverable is missing, and that might not read your copy.` Four artifacts qualify as §3.4 stands, each read off its column 3 rather than carried here: `idea.md`, whose one row is `/create-prd`'s idea ladder; `epic.md`, whose rows have `/create-ard` and `/specify` at Epic altitude read the Epic folder as it stands and `/dev-workflows:conformance` trace what exists; the ARD, whose consumers all fall back to `status: none` and `ard-resolution.md`'s no-regression rule — on a multi-component PRD, `/epics` and `/implement` also ask whether to land it first, each offering to continue (`${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/references/components.md` §6), which that rule states as its one exception; and `design.md`, gated in-scope-only by `/implement`, recorded as a coverage gap by `/ready` and left out of what `/dev-workflows:conformance` traces. **What a fallback does with the un-landed copy is the consumer's, and the clause promises neither way**: `/create-prd` names an un-landed `idea.md` and does not read it in contract — it reaches it only through its same-session rung or a path the operator types, and its `@<path>` form reads it directly (§3.4's row); an ARD on no ref resolves `status: none`, so its consumers read no ARD at all and say nothing about it (`ard-resolution.md`, *Output*); and `/implement` reads an in-scope `design.md` exactly as it did before the gate, while `/ready` records it missing; `/create-ard` and `/specify` read an un-landed `epic.md` from the Epic folder and report it. The clause read *"reports the artifact as un-landed and proceeds from the resolved folder"* until it was checked against those rows, and for the artifact it was written for it promised a read that happens only out of contract: `/create-prd` does name the file, and then goes down its idea ladder, which reaches the brief only through its same-session rung or a typed path, and otherwise grills the PRD without it.
- **advisory** → `Nothing stops on this; the phase that reads it reads your working copy, so it still sees this run's result.`
- **unread** → `Nothing downstream reads it, so no command stops on this.`

**Row F is the next phase's reading only where the artifact was on no ref before this run.** A run that edited a copy `<default-ref>` already carried — a refine, an amendment, an annotation — and is declined leaves a working copy that differs from the merged one, and every gate meets that at §3.3's rows C′, C″ or C, ahead of row F: a stop, or a repair offer that ends in one. So such a run takes the **stopping** half whatever the artifact's rows say, and a producer whose runs can do either selects per run — on whether `<default-ref>` already carries a declared path of its falling-back artifact (`git -C "$SPECS_PATH" cat-file -e "<default-ref>:./<path>"`, §3.2's primitive), tested before the offer. `/idea` on its refine path, `/create-ard` refining an ARD, `/implement` Phase 4.5 annotating a merged `design.md` and `/epics` re-drafting a merged Epic are the producers that meet it; each said the next phase would not stop until this sentence was written.

**The PRD is what the quantifier was written for, and it moves out of the falling-back bullet.** It stood there on the strength of `/create-ard`'s and `/specify`'s rows while `/prd-ground` **(idea route)** and `/prd-proposal` each mint a `*_PRD_NOT_HANDED_OFF` stop for exactly the state a decline leaves — so a `/create-prd` or `/update-prd` run that declined reported *"the next phase does not stop on that"* about a file two commands refuse with a stop id minted for it. Read the rows; never carry either membership list above.

**A `deliverable_paths` set spanning both halves takes the stopping one** — §4.0's strongest-class rule carried one level down, and the reason `/design` prints the stopping clause: its set carries the amended `specification.md`, which `/design` itself stops on, beside a `design.md` nothing stops on. **A producer whose set varies between runs resolves this per run**, and two do: `/create-ard` (the ARD alone, or the ARD beside `grounding/` files and `decisions.md`) and `/implement` Phase 4.5 (an annotated `design.md` alone, or `specification.md` with it).

No two of the four are interchangeable, and each wrong pick misleads in its own direction: the stop clause **on an artifact nothing stops on** promises a refusal the operator will not meet, the fallback clause describes a fallback by a phase that was never waiting on the file, the advisory clause tells them a reader exists where none does, and the unread clause tells them to ignore a phase that is in fact reading the file. Telling them apart costs nothing — the producer knows which artifact it just wrote, and §4.0 says which class it is in.

### 4.2 The no-`gh` fallback text

    The branch is pushed but no pull request was opened (<reason>).
    Open one from <branch> into <default> in the web UI, using this title:
      <title>
    The body is at <body-path>.
    <downstream-clause>   # §4.1, resolved from the artifact's §4.0 class — never the bare
                          # "until it is merged" sentence, which is false for both the
                          # advisory and the unread class.

### 4.3 The consent choice

**One array per `<next-phase-clause>` value (§4.1) — four, not three, and the count is derived rather than asserted.** §4.0 has three classes and §4.1 splits the *gated* one in two on §3.4's own column, so **§4.1's bullet list is the authority on how many arrays this section carries**; each array below names the bullet it pairs with, and an edit that adds or retires a clause value adds or retires its array in the same change. A producing command presents the array its artifact's clause selects, verbatim — order, wording, and the `(Recommended)` marker are not the caller's to change. Only the second option's parenthetical differs between the four; the first and third options are identical in all of them. (Quoting these arrays into a command is sanctioned, and is the one thing §5 rule 4 exempts from its "never restate this reference" rule — an array is user-facing text the harness renders literally, not a rule. That exemption carries one obligation, and it falls on the citing form only: a command that *cites* this array rather than quoting it names the class it cites for — and, where that class is **gated**, which of its two arrays, because naming the class alone no longer picks one.)

**This section stood at three arrays against §4.1's four, which is why the count is tied to that list instead of restated here.** The asymmetry had already been found and fixed once, at three clause values against a single array, on the reasoning that *the array is shown before the decision and the clause after it, so the array is the half that must not under-describe*; the later commit that split the gated clause in two then left this section at the class count, re-creating it at four-against-three. The cost fell on `/idea`, which promised a stop `/create-prd` does not make. A section carrying a different number of arrays from §4.1's bullets is the defect, not a formatting difference.

**Selecting an array is not the whole of this section, and a producer that takes only its array offers a `(Recommended)` push it may be unable to run.** Three steps below run **before** whichever array is selected here: the flag line a run carrying `specs_git: blocked` or `specs_git: misrooted` prints (*Before anything else*), §2.1's push-target probe, and the no-remote line that probe decides (*Before presenting the array*). They are written after the arrays because all three are identical for all four, and they are named here because a reader who finds their class, copies its array and stops never reaches them — which is exactly how a producer came to present a push-and-open-PR option, marked `(Recommended)`, on a repository with no `origin` and with no notice above it, the live state §2.1 records that probe as having been added for.

**The obvious remedy — a copy of the probe step beside each quoted array — was measured and refused, and the measurement is recorded here so it is not re-proposed without new evidence.** Re-derive it with `grep -n 'Branch + commit + push + open PR to main' plugins/*/commands/*.md` and read the lines above each hit: every inlined copy of these arrays in the family is preceded, within its handoff section, by the `Skill(skill: "workflows-core:reference", args: "phase-handoff handoff-to-main")` request that loads `handoff-to-main`'s own file, which holds this section — so a producer presenting an array has this section open, and the probe and its notice are reached from exactly where the copier lands. A copy at each producer would restate a rule the caller contract's never-restate rule forbids restating, whose one exception is the arrays themselves and nothing around them, and it would put the probe's wording in as many places as there are producers to keep in step. What is *not* covered by that measurement, and is review's: a producer that presents an array it never loaded this section to get.

**gated — stopping** (§4.1 bullet 1) — some consumer stops on this artifact, by a §3.4 row or by its own guard; `architecture/**` is the guard's case, with `/harvest-decisions` and `/promote-decisions` its producers:

    choices: ["Branch + commit + push + open PR to main (Recommended)", "Just write the files — I'll handle git (the next phase will stop until this is on main)", "Cancel"]

**gated — falling back** (§4.1 bullet 2) — a consumer runs `require-on-main` on it, but **every** §3.4 row naming it preserves a pre-existing absent behaviour, so row F delegates rather than stops — and only on a run whose copy of it `<default-ref>` did not already carry, since a declined edit of a merged copy meets the C rows first (§4.1, *Row F is the next phase's reading only where …*). `idea.md` is the case and `/idea` the producer; the ARD and `design.md` are two more artifacts, reached by a producer whose whole set is one of them; and `epic.md` is the fourth, whose producer `/epics` presents this array for a set whose other paths stop nothing — `_coverage.md`, unread, and any index page its Documentation agent edits and the PRD folder's `CLAUDE.md` its Instructions agent edits, both advisory (§4.0) — on a run whose Epics are all new or unchanged. The parenthetical promises no read, because §4.1's bullet shows that most of those fallbacks do not read the un-landed copy:

    choices: ["Branch + commit + push + open PR to main (Recommended)", "Just write the files — I'll handle git (the next phase does not stop on this, but until this is on main it might not read your copy)", "Cancel"]

**advisory** (§4.1 bullet 3) — nothing gates it, but a command reads it. `_readiness.md` is the case, and `/ready` the producer, for a set whose other paths take no stronger class — the folder's `CLAUDE.md` its Instructions agent edits and any page its Documentation agent edits, both advisory (§4.0):

    choices: ["Branch + commit + push + open PR to main (Recommended)", "Just write the files — I'll handle git (no command stops on this; what reads it reads your working copy)", "Cancel"]

**unread** (§4.1 bullet 4) — nothing gates it and nothing reads it after the run that wrote it. §4.0's register now names its members: `/update-prd`'s and `/create-prd`'s archived PRD revision, `/epics`' `_coverage.md`, and — out of the proposal pair's deliverable sets — either command's `proposal-brief.md` and either command's archived proposal revisions. The two term records, `/specify`'s `_glossary.md` and `/design`'s `_design-glossary.md`, left the class another way: they had no reader until `/design`'s interface fan-out began reading them, and adding a reader moves an artifact's row. **This class has lost a member every time someone actually looked**: the frame-set index, which `design-grounder` refuses to run without; `slices.md`, which `/brd-reconcile` corrects in place; three artifacts a later run of the command that wrote them reads — the `BRD-` umbrella's own `proposal.md`, `/specify`'s `_session.md` and `/design`'s `_design-session.md`; and the documentation page a pre-handoff Documentation agent edits, which `/brd-reconcile`'s stale cross-reference sweep reads. A producer reaching for this array is making the claim every one of those failed: that it looked for a reader and there is none. Look, before selecting it — in this run's own folder as well as downstream, since a later run of the producing command is a reader like any other:

    choices: ["Branch + commit + push + open PR to main (Recommended)", "Just write the files — I'll handle git (nothing downstream reads this, so no command stops on it)", "Cancel"]

The second option's parenthetical is load-bearing: it is the only place the user learns what declining costs, and the only reason there are four arrays rather than one. It must agree with the `<next-phase-clause>` §4.1 prints on that same decline — the two are read by the same operator minutes apart, and a run that contradicts its own prompt teaches them to trust neither half. **That agreement is why the two lists are one list**: a fourth clause value with no fourth array here cannot be agreed with by any array a producer is allowed to present. Each wrong pick misleads in its own direction — one per array, the same four §4.1 lists for its clauses: the stopping-gated array promises a refusal the operator will not meet, the falling-back one describes a fallback by a phase that was never waiting on the file, the advisory one tells them a reader exists where none does, and the unread array tells them to ignore a phase that is reading the file.

**Select by §4.0's test, never by "has a §3.4 row" alone — then, inside *gated*, by §4.1's quantifier.** A missing row rules out §3.4 gating — a consumer's own guard still makes the artifact gated — and otherwise decides nothing between **advisory** and **unread**; the producer settles that by naming the reader, or by naming that there is none. A row present settles *gated* and still leaves two arrays: the stopping one unless **every** row naming the artifact falls back. Both halves of the old binary were wrong about `_readiness.md` at once: `/ready` presented the gated array for an artifact no command gates, and the alternate it should have fallen to under the "no §3.4 row" test would have told the operator that nothing downstream reads a file `/implement` Phase 0.5 reads on every keyed run.

**Before anything else, read the run's flags.** Where the run carries `specs_git: blocked` or `specs_git: misrooted`, §2.1's gate will refuse the first option whatever the repository holds. Print one line immediately above the array, in place of the no-remote line below, then present the array itself unchanged:

    This run carries specs_git: <blocked | misrooted> (<a detached HEAD in the specs repository | a misplaced SPECS_PATH>), so the first option will be refused: nothing is committed, pushed or opened, and the deliverable stays written and uncommitted whichever option you pick.

The array keeps its wording and its `(Recommended)` marker, because a phase's array is presented verbatim (`workflows-core:escalation-rules`, *Choice lists are presented verbatim*). The line is what tells the operator that the marker does not hold on this run, as the no-remote line does for a push. Option 1 then reaches §2.1, whose gate failure §4.1's *Gate failed* row reports; options 2 and 3 print the *Declined by the user* row as always. The flags are run state that §2.1's gate also reads, and reading them runs nothing of §2, so the probe below is still the one step of §2 that runs ahead of the choice.

**Before presenting the array, run §2.1's push-target probe.** It is read-only — `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" remote get-url origin` — and it is the one step of §2 that runs ahead of the choice, because its result is what decides the line below; `handoff-to-main` carries the `remote` value it set into §2.5 and §2.6 when option 1 is taken. Where `git -C "$SPECS_PATH" rev-parse --git-dir` fails there is no repository to probe: print nothing here, and §2.1's gate reports that state if option 1 is taken. **Where the probe set `remote: none` and no flag line was printed above, print one line immediately above the array**, then present the array itself unchanged:

    This specs repo has no `origin` remote: the first option will branch and commit locally, and the push and pull request cannot run.

The array is not reworded for this, and that is deliberate rather than lazy. The option text says what the option is *for*; the class parenthetical is already the only thing that varies between the arrays above, and making the option line vary on the remote as well would be one more literal string per array for every producer to keep in step — to carry a fact about the *repository*, which every class shares, rather than about the artifact, which is what the class distinguishes. **That cost is stated per array rather than as a number, for the reason this section's opening gives**: the count is §4.1's bullet list to fix, and a second copy of it here is exactly how this paragraph came to say *three* while the section it sits in carried four. The line above the array is where the operator meets that fact, at the moment they choose, which is exactly what this section's agreement principle asks for; §4.1's *No remote* row then reports the same fact when the run finishes. The first option keeps its `(Recommended)` marker: committing the deliverable locally is still the best of the three options, and the notice has already said what it will and will not do.

**What each option means.** Option 1 runs `handoff-to-main` (§2). Options 2 and 3 both decline it: the deliverable stays written and uncommitted, and the producer emits §4.1's "Declined by the user" line either way. They differ only in recorded intent — option 2 states the user will handle git themselves, option 3 states nothing — so a caller must not infer from option 3 that the artifact is unwanted, and must never delete or revert it. **Neither option stops the run's emitter tail**: feedback → follow-ups → cost → `resume.md` → `commit-artifacts` still executes, because that tail commits only `$SPECS_PATH`'s bounded session-artifact paths (`specs-repo-git.md` §2.1), never the deliverable this choice governs.
